topic: Day 2 · Localising the Bleed — Colonoscopy, CT Angiography & Scintigraphy
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Endoscopy & GI Bleed Service
speakerBio: Endoscopist who co-runs the joint GI–interventional radiology bleeding pathway and teaches trainees to match the diagnostic tool to the patient's haemodynamics rather than to the loudest phone call.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 76-year-old man is bleeding — bright red clots, ongoing, HR 122, BP 88/50 despite two units of red cells and a litre of crystalloid. The night registrar has phoned the on-call endoscopist to "come and scope him now." The endoscopist asks one question that changes the whole night: "Is he stable, and is his colon prepped?" He is neither. This session is about matching the diagnostic weapon to the patient: colonoscopy, CT angiography, catheter mesenteric angiography, and red-cell scintigraphy each detect a different rate of bleeding and offer different things — some only look, some also treat. Choose wrong and you either miss the source or, worse, send an exsanguinating patient into an unprepped colonoscopy that cannot possibly help.

1 · 🧠 The organising principle — rate, timing, and treat-vs-look

Every localisation decision turns on three questions:

  1. How fast is it bleeding? Each modality has a threshold bleeding rate below which it sees nothing — this is the single most important number for each test.
  2. Is it bleeding right now? The angiographic and nuclear tests need active extravasation at the moment of imaging; colonoscopy can find a lesion (a visible vessel, adherent clot) even after bleeding has paused.
  3. Do I want to LOOK or also TREAT? Colonoscopy and catheter angiography are diagnostic AND therapeutic; CT angiography and scintigraphy only localise — they are a map, not a cure.
Ask of every test: what is the slowest bleed it can see, does it need active bleeding, and can it also stop the bleed? Those three answers pick the tool.

2 · 🔬 Colonoscopy — the diagnostic and therapeutic cornerstone

For the stable patient, colonoscopy is the first-line investigation and, per the ACG 2016 guideline, the recommended initial test in most acute LGIB. Its great advantage is that it is both diagnostic and therapeutic — you can see the lesion and clip, coagulate, band, or inject it in the same sitting — and it does not require the patient to be actively bleeding at the moment of the procedure.

The timing debate — early vs elective

  • ACG 2016: for high-risk patients (haemodynamic instability, ongoing bleeding), perform colonoscopy within 24 hours of presentation after adequate resuscitation and a rapid bowel purge.
  • However, randomised trials (e.g. the "urgent vs elective colonoscopy" studies) have NOT shown that very early/urgent colonoscopy improves mortality, rebleeding, or the need for surgery compared with elective (next-available, e.g. ≤72h) colonoscopy. Urgent scoping increases diagnostic yield of a definite source but has not translated into better hard outcomes.
  • Practical synthesis: resuscitate, risk-stratify, and aim for colonoscopy within 24h in genuinely high-risk stable patients, but do not force an emergency scope on an unprepared or unstable colon just for speed.

The bowel-prep problem

⚠️ You cannot see through blood and stool

An unprepped colon is opaque — retained blood, clot, and faeces obscure the mucosa, tank the diagnostic yield, raise the perforation risk, and can miss the very lesion you came for. Adequate visualisation needs a rapid purge (e.g. 4–6 L of polyethylene glycol over 3–4 hours, often via NG tube). This takes time — which is precisely why the haemodynamically unstable, actively bleeding patient, who cannot wait for or tolerate a prep, should NOT go straight to colonoscopy. They go to CT angiography.

3 · 🖥️ CT angiography — fast, non-invasive, needs active bleeding

CT angiography (CTA) has become the pivotal test in the unstable or actively bleeding patient. It is fast, widely available out-of-hours, requires no bowel prep, and non-invasively localises the bleeding point as a blush of contrast extravasating into the lumen — providing a road-map for the interventional radiologist or surgeon.

  • Detects active bleeding at roughly 0.3–0.5 mL/min.
  • Purely diagnostic / localising — it does not treat; a positive CTA is the trigger to proceed to catheter angiography for embolisation, or to targeted surgery.
  • Best performed while the patient is actively bleeding — a negative scan in a patient who has transiently stopped simply means the tap was off at that moment.
  • Costs: contrast nephropathy risk and radiation — but in a shocked bleeder these are readily justified.
💡 CTA is the triage test of the unstable bleeder

In the actively bleeding, unstable patient (after an upper source is excluded), CTA is the fast first step: it says whether there is active extravasation and where, letting IR go straight to the culprit vessel rather than hunting blindly. A positive CTA → catheter angiography ± embolisation.

4 · 🎯 Catheter mesenteric angiography — localise AND embolise

Conventional catheter mesenteric angiography is the interventional step: the radiologist selectively catheterises the SMA/IMA, identifies the extravasating vessel, and can then perform super-selective embolisation to stop the bleed in the same procedure.

  • Requires a brisker bleed to see the blush — roughly 0.5–1.0 mL/min. Less sensitive than CTA or scintigraphy, but uniquely therapeutic.
  • Because it is less sensitive, it is often guided by a positive CTA — CTA finds and localises, then angiography targets and treats.
  • Risks: contrast load, access-site complications, and — critically — bowel ischaemia from over-embolisation (covered in depth in session 12).

5 · ☢️ Red-cell scintigraphy — the most sensitive, but only a region

Technetium-99m-labelled red-cell scintigraphy (a nuclear medicine scan) is the most sensitive test for GI bleeding — it can detect very slow bleeding, around 0.1–0.4 mL/min, and because the labelled cells persist, the patient can be re-imaged over hours to catch intermittent bleeding.

  • Best for slow, obscure, or intermittent bleeding that CTA and colonoscopy keep missing.
  • Major limitation: it only localises to a broad region (e.g. "right lower quadrant"), not a precise vessel or segment, and pooled/moving intraluminal blood can mislead. It is diagnostic only — never therapeutic.
  • Often used to decide whether an angiogram is worthwhile, or to guide the segment for surgery/endoscopy.

💡 Memory hook — the sensitivity ladder

From slowest bleed detectable to fastest required: scintigraphy (0.1) → CTA (0.3–0.5) → catheter angiography (0.5–1.0). Scintigraphy sees the faintest trickle but only points to a region; catheter angiography needs a brisker bleed but is the only one of the three that can also treat. Colonoscopy sits outside the rate ladder because it hunts lesions, not flow.

7 · 🗺️ The algorithm — stable vs unstable

Everything collapses into one fork: is the patient haemodynamically stable?

PathwayStable patientUnstable / ongoing brisk bleeding
Exclude upper sourceConsider if features suggest itYes — NG aspirate / OGD first
First localising testColonoscopy after bowel prep (within 24h if high-risk)CT angiography (no prep, no delay)
If positiveTreat endoscopically in the same sitting→ Catheter angiography + embolisation (or targeted surgery)
If negative / obscureRepeat colonoscopy; red-cell scintigraphy; small-bowel work-up (capsule, enteroscopy)Red-cell scintigraphy; consider surgery if exsanguinating and localised
Stable colon → colonoscopy after prep. Unstable, still bleeding → CT angiography, then interventional radiology. The unstable patient does not get an unprepped colonoscopy.
🎯 Why the unstable patient skips the scope

Three reasons converge. (1) There is no time to give and clear a 4–6 L bowel prep in someone who is shocked and bleeding. (2) An unprepped, blood-filled colon defeats the endoscopist's view, so the yield plummets and perforation risk rises. (3) CTA answers the two questions that actually matter fastest — is it still bleeding, and where? — and hands the interventional radiologist a target for embolisation. The scope has its moment; that moment is after resuscitation, in a stable, prepped patient.

8 · 🧩 Matching the clinical picture to the test

  • Stable, bleeding settled, first presentation: elective colonoscopy after prep — diagnostic + therapeutic, excludes cancer.
  • Stable but high-risk (ongoing ooze, comorbid): resuscitate, purge, colonoscopy within 24h.
  • Unstable, actively bleeding: exclude upper source → CTA → catheter angiography ± embolisation; surgery if uncontrolled and localised.
  • Recurrent, obscure, or intermittent: red-cell scintigraphy (most sensitive; can re-image), and small-bowel evaluation (capsule endoscopy, CT/MR enterography, device-assisted enteroscopy, Meckel's scan in the young).
☠️ M&M — the unprepped colonoscopy in a shocked patient

A 74-year-old woman with brisk ongoing haematochezia, HR 130 and BP 82/44 after 3 units of red cells, was taken directly to the endoscopy suite for an "urgent colonoscopy" without resuscitation to stability and without any bowel prep. The colon was full of blood and clot; the endoscopist could not identify a source, the procedure was prolonged, and during insufflation the patient became more hypotensive and desaturated, requiring intubation. No source was found, no therapy was delivered, and she then went for CT angiography anyway — which immediately showed a right-colic branch blush that was embolised successfully. Lessons: (1) the unstable, actively bleeding patient should have gone to CT angiography first, not an unprepped scope; (2) an unprepped, blood-filled colon has a dismal diagnostic yield and real procedural risk; (3) urgency is not served by choosing a test that cannot see — CTA localised in minutes what the scope could not in an hour; (4) the correct sequence — resuscitate, exclude upper source, CTA, then IR — would have reached the same successful embolisation without the airway crisis. Speed applied to the wrong tool is just a faster way to fail.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Pick the test by three questions: what is the slowest bleed it sees, does it need active bleeding, and can it also treat?
  2. Colonoscopy is first-line in the stable patient — diagnostic AND therapeutic, not rate-dependent, but needs a prepped colon; aim within 24h if high-risk.
  3. Urgent colonoscopy improves diagnostic yield but not mortality/rebleeding/surgery versus elective — don't force an emergency scope for speed alone.
  4. CT angiography (~0.3–0.5 mL/min) is the triage test of the unstable, actively bleeding patient — fast, no prep, localises for IR/surgery, but only maps.
  5. Catheter angiography (~0.5–1.0 mL/min) localises AND embolises — the therapeutic radiologic step, usually CTA-guided.
  6. Red-cell scintigraphy (~0.1–0.4 mL/min) is the most sensitive but localises only to a region and never treats — reserve for slow/intermittent/obscure bleeds.
  7. The unstable patient goes to CTA/angiography, never to an unprepped colonoscopy.

moderatorQs.q: Rank colonoscopy, CT angiography, catheter angiography and red-cell scintigraphy by the bleeding rate each can detect, and say which can also treat.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: By sensitivity to slow bleeding, from most to least sensitive: red-cell scintigraphy (~0.1–0.4 mL/min) > CT angiography (~0.3–0.5 mL/min) > catheter mesenteric angiography (~0.5–1.0 mL/min). Colonoscopy sits outside this rate ladder because it detects lesions and stigmata rather than a flow rate, so it can find a source even after bleeding has stopped. Crucially, only two of these can also treat: colonoscopy (clips, thermal coagulation, banding, adrenaline) and catheter angiography (super-selective embolisation). CTA and scintigraphy are purely diagnostic road-maps — scintigraphy is the most sensitive but only localises to a broad region, while CTA gives a precise site and is the practical triage test of the unstable, actively bleeding patient.

moderatorQs.q: An unstable patient is actively bleeding. Why not just do a colonoscopy urgently, and what is the correct sequence?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because an urgent colonoscopy in this setting usually fails and can harm. There is no time to give and clear the 4–6 L bowel prep a decent view requires, and an unprepped, blood-filled colon defeats visualisation — diagnostic yield collapses and perforation risk rises, all while the patient continues to bleed. The correct sequence is: resuscitate to whatever stability you can, exclude an upper source (NG aspirate / OGD), then CT angiography to answer 'is it still bleeding and where'; a positive CTA sends the patient to catheter angiography for super-selective embolisation, with targeted surgery reserved for uncontrolled, localised bleeding. Colonoscopy's role comes later, in the stable, prepped patient. Speed must be spent on a test that can actually see and treat.

moderatorQs.q: Does performing colonoscopy urgently (within 24h) rather than electively improve outcomes?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It improves the diagnostic yield — you are more likely to catch active bleeding or fresh stigmata and identify a definite source — but the randomised evidence has not shown a benefit in the hard outcomes of mortality, rebleeding, or need for surgery compared with elective (e.g. next-available, within ~72h) colonoscopy. The ACG 2016 guideline still recommends colonoscopy within 24 hours for high-risk patients after adequate resuscitation and bowel purge, because early localisation and endoscopic therapy are reasonable, but the take-home is that you should not force an emergency, poorly-prepped scope purely for speed. Resuscitation, risk stratification, and adequate prep matter more than shaving hours off the timing.

audienceQs.q: If red-cell scintigraphy is the most sensitive test, why don't we just use it for everyone?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because sensitivity isn't the only thing that matters. Scintigraphy detects the slowest bleeds (~0.1–0.4 mL/min) and can re-image over hours to catch intermittent bleeding, but it has two big drawbacks: it only localises to a broad region (e.g. 'right lower quadrant'), not a specific vessel or segment — and pooled or moving intraluminal blood can mislead you — and it is purely diagnostic, never therapeutic. It's also slower to organise and needs nuclear medicine availability. So in the unstable patient you want CTA (precise site, fast) leading to angiographic embolisation (treats); in the stable patient you want colonoscopy (precise lesion, treats). Scintigraphy earns its place in the slow, obscure, or intermittent bleed that the other tests keep missing.

audienceQs.q: How much active bleeding does the patient need for CT angiography to show something?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Roughly 0.3–0.5 mL/min of active extravasation at the moment of the scan — that's the rate at which contrast blushes visibly into the bowel lumen. The key practical corollary is that CTA is a snapshot: the patient must be bleeding during the acquisition, so a negative study in someone who has transiently stopped doesn't exclude a significant intermittent source — it just means the tap was off. That's why timing matters: scan them while they're actively bleeding. For comparison, catheter angiography needs a somewhat brisker bleed (~0.5–1.0 mL/min) but can embolise, whereas red-cell scintigraphy will pick up slower bleeding (~0.1 mL/min) but only regionally. A positive CTA is your cue to call interventional radiology.

audienceQs.q: The patient keeps bleeding but every test has been negative or only 'regional'. Can I take them to theatre?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Only with the best localisation you can get first — operating on an unlocalised lower GI bleed is dangerous (it forces the surgeon toward a blind subtotal colectomy with high morbidity, covered in the next session). So exhaust localisation: repeat CT angiography while actively bleeding, red-cell scintigraphy for slow/intermittent bleeding, and a small-bowel work-up (capsule, CT/MR enterography, enteroscopy; a Meckel's scan in a younger patient) to make sure the source isn't beyond the colonoscope's reach. If the patient is truly exsanguinating and a segment has been identified (even regionally on scintigraphy or CTA), a targeted segmental resection is far safer than a blind colectomy. The surgical decision should be a joint one with gastroenterology and interventional radiology, and embolisation is often the better bridge than the knife.
